description: Shredded green papaya salad mixed with long beans, tomato, peanuts, and dried shrimp, combined in a mortar and served fresh.
where_you_will_see_it:
Street carts and small open-air stalls where it is made to order
Food courts and casual restaurants, often listed among noodle and rice dishes
when_its_eaten:
Eaten as a main dish or shared side rather than a light snack
Common at lunch and dinner, especially in casual settings
how_people_usually_eat_it:
Stirred lightly before eating to redistribute the dressing at the bottom
Eaten alongside sticky rice, which is used to scoop or balance bites
Adjusted with extra chilli, fish sauce, or sugar if those are set out
why_its_popular: It is quick to prepare, highly adjustable, and fits easily alongside many other dishes.
first_impressions:
More intense than expected
Very crunchy
Strong smell on arrival
Feels light but filling
Memorable even in small portions
good_to_know:
The name breaks down as som (sour) and tam (to pound), describing both the flavour profile and the mortar-based mixing.
Spice levels vary widely by vendor unless specified when ordering.
preparation:
Raw green papaya is shredded and placed in a mortar where it is lightly pounded with long beans and tomato so the vegetables bruise and release moisture.

Dressing ingredients are added and coat the strands evenly, creating a crisp salad that softens slightly as it sits and is eaten immediately with visible liquid pooling at the bottom.
ingredients:
Green Papaya
Long Beans
Tomato
Garlic
Chilli
Fish Sauce
Palm Sugar
Lime
Dried Shrimp
Peanuts
